title: Why You Should Never Kneel Down Eye Level With Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin directly contradicts a widely recommended practice -- kneeling to a student's eye level to discuss behavior -- arguing it's both physically dangerous and counterproductive to influence. On safety, he points to the frequency of teachers being physically assaulted by students and argues that kneeling within striking distance during a behavior conversation is an unnecessary vulnerability. On effectiveness, he argues that invading a student's personal space reads as threatening or hostile even when done kindly, especially for older students, and typically produces compliance-in-appearance (telling the teacher what they want to hear) rather than real influence, ultimately reducing trust rather than building it. His alternative is procedural rather than relational: keep a consistent physical distance always, and rely on a transparent, fully pre-taught classroom management plan -- where students already know exactly what will happen for any rule violation -- so that in-the-moment personal conversations about behavior become unnecessary altogether. He frames this as both a safer and a more effective path to influence than physical closeness.
points: Kneeling to a student's eye level during behavior discussions puts the teacher within striking distance, given how often teachers report being physically assaulted by students.
Invading a student's personal space reads as threatening or hostile even when done kindly, and typically produces surface compliance rather than genuine influence.
Keep a consistent physical distance at all times rather than crowding into personal space, kneeling or otherwise.
A fully pre-taught, transparent classroom management plan makes in-the-moment personal conversations about behavior largely unnecessary in the first place.
quotes: Kneeling down to a student’s eye level to discuss behavior or impart an important lesson is common practice.
SCM is a vessel for teacher horror stories. We hear it all, from teachers being accused of false crimes to their cars getting keyed in the parking lot.
You must protect your safety. And nothing puts you in a more vulnerable position than kneeling down within striking distance. Add to it a discussion about misbehavior and you’re asking for trouble.
But placing yourself inside a student’s personal space is threatening and hostile, especially if you put your hands on them (which is a no-no).
They definitely won’t listen to you, other than than to tell you what you want to hear. Afterward, you’ll have less influence over their behavior, not more.
First, make a rule for yourself to never crowd into a student’s personal space, kneeling or otherwise. Always keep a safe distance.
